name: Capstone Project: Build Your AI Business Plan, Service, Automation, Marketing Strategy or Productivity System
objectives: Given the five capstone choices and a real business, choose one project and write a one-paragraph scope with what is in, what is out and a finish date, small enough to finish on time

Given your project's main assumptions, interview at least three real people with neutral questions and mark each assumption confirmed, wrong or unsure, recording their exact words and updating the scope when an assumption is wrong
Given your scope and validation notes, write an outline with the right sections for your project type, marking which sections need your own facts
Using AI as your assistant, build the project one section at a time with AI drafting and you checking, keeping a build log and using placeholders for private details
Given your project, check its numbers in a spreadsheet and write a risk checklist, with every formula checked and tax and legal items marked to confirm with an official source or professional
Given your finished project, test it with three people, make the top changes and give a three-minute presentation, covering the problem, your solution, the proof and the next step

lessons.title: Lesson 1: Stage 1: Choosing and scoping your project
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Choose one of the five capstone projects and write a one-paragraph scope.
This lesson builds toward: Given the five capstone choices and a real business, you will choose one project and write a one-paragraph scope with what is in, what is out and a finish date, small enough to finish on time.
Pick the project that will help a real business most in the next three months. A business plan fits a new idea that needs a clear plan or funding. A service business fits someone ready to sell a service using AI. An automation system fits a business drowning in repeated tasks. A marketing strategy fits a business that needs more customers. A productivity ecosystem fits an owner who is overwhelmed and needs a better week.
Scope means deciding what is in and what is out. A good scope is small enough to finish: "A 90-day marketing strategy for my mobile car wash, focused on one neighborhood and two channels" is better than "marketing for everything".
Ask AI to help you compare: "Here is my business and my biggest problem. Which of these five capstone projects would help most, and why?" Then decide yourself and write your scope.
Step by step:
- Write your business (or the one you are helping) and its biggest problem.
- Read the five project choices.
- Ask AI which would help most and why.
- Choose one.
- Write a one-paragraph scope: what is in, what is out, and the finish date.
Words to know:
- Capstone: a final project that brings together everything you learned.
- Scope: the limits of a project: what is included and what is not.
Try it now: Choose your capstone project and write a one-paragraph scope with what is in, what is out and your finish date.
You can now choose a capstone project that fits a real business and scope it so you can finish it.

check.q: What does a project scope say?
options: What is in and out of the project, and when it will be done
Every idea you have ever had
The name of your AI tool
check.why: A scope keeps the project small enough to finish.

check.q: Your scope covers marketing in five cities and six channels in two weeks. What do you do?
options: Narrow it to one area and a few channels
check.why: A smaller scope can be finished and done well.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Stage 2: Validating with real people
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Check your project's assumptions by talking to at least three real people.
This lesson builds toward: Given your project's main assumptions, you will interview at least three real people with neutral questions and mark each assumption confirmed, wrong or unsure, recording their exact words and updating the scope when an assumption is wrong.
Every project rests on assumptions: customers want this, they will pay this much, this task wastes this many hours, people find us on this platform. Validation means checking them with real people before you build.
Ask AI: "List the five biggest assumptions in this project and write three neutral interview questions for each." Neutral means you do not lead the person: ask "How do you handle this today?" not "Wouldn't you love my idea?"
Talk to at least three people: possible customers, the business owner, or staff who do the work. Write their exact words. Then ask AI to help you group what you heard, and note which assumptions held up and which did not.
Step by step:
- Ask AI to list your project's five biggest assumptions.
- Write neutral interview questions.
- Talk to at least three real people.
- Write down their exact words.
- Mark each assumption: confirmed, wrong or unsure, and update your scope.
Words to know:
- Assumption: something you believe is true but have not checked.
- Validation: checking assumptions with real evidence before you build.
- Neutral question: a question that does not push the person toward an answer.
Try it now: List your five assumptions with AI's help, interview at least three people with neutral questions, and mark each assumption confirmed, wrong or unsure.
You can now validate a business project with real people before building it.

check.q: What is an assumption in a business project?
options: Something you believe but have not checked
check.why: Validation checks assumptions with real people.

check.q: An interview shows customers do not care about the feature you planned around. What do you do?
check.why: Wrong assumptions should change the plan before you build.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Stage 3: Designing the solution
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Write the outline of your project using the right structure for your choice.
This lesson builds toward: Given your scope and validation notes, you will write an outline with the right sections for your project type, marking which sections need your own facts.
Each project has a structure. Business plan: the SBA lists traditional plan sections (executive summary, company description, market analysis, organization and management, service or product line, marketing and sales, funding request, financial projections) and a lean plan option. Service business: the problem, the deliverable, the steps (AI and human), the instruction prompt, the price. Automation system: the workflow map, trigger and actions, AI step, approval guardrails, tests and monitoring.
Marketing strategy: ideal customer, offer, one or two channels, a content calendar, an email plan, and the numbers you will track. Productivity ecosystem: the week plan, the toolkit (one tool per job), templates, SOPs, automations and a time log.
Ask AI to turn your scope and validation notes into an outline with these sections. Edit it so every section reflects what real people told you.
Step by step:
- Find the structure for your project type.
- Give AI your scope and validation notes.
- Ask for an outline with those sections and one line on what goes in each.
- Edit the outline using what real people told you.
- Mark which sections AI can draft and which need your own facts.
Words to know:
- Outline: the list of sections a project will have, before you write it fully.
- Lean plan: a short business plan focused on the key parts, as an alternative to a long traditional plan.
Official sources:
- SBA: Write your business plan
Try it now: Have AI turn your scope and validation notes into an outline with the right sections for your project. Edit it and mark which sections need your own facts.
You can now design the full structure of your capstone project based on real evidence.

check.q: Where can you find the standard sections of a business plan?
check.why: The SBA lists traditional business plan sections.

check.q: AI's outline for your automation project leaves out guardrails. What do you do?
check.why: An automation project needs workflow, trigger and actions, AI step, guardrails and tests.

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Stage 4: Building it with AI
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Build the full project section by section, with AI drafting and you checking.
This lesson builds toward: Using AI as your assistant, you will build the project one section at a time with AI drafting and you checking, keeping a build log and using placeholders for private details.
Work one section at a time. For each, give AI the section name, your real facts and the format you want. Example: "Write the market analysis section for my mobile car wash business plan. Here is what three customers told me and the local facts I found. Under 300 words, plain language."
For hands-on projects, build the real thing: set up the automation and test it, create the templates and SOPs, make the first posts and the email, or write the service package and run it once.
Keep a short build log: what you made, which tool, what you changed after checking. Never put private customer or money details into AI tools; use placeholders and fill them in yourself.
Step by step:
- Pick the next section from your outline.
- Give AI the section name, your facts and the format.
- Check the draft: facts, numbers, tone, claims.
- Build hands-on parts for real and test them.
- Write a line in your build log and move to the next section.
Words to know:
- Build log: a simple record of what you made, with which tool, and what you changed.
- Placeholder: a stand-in like [customer name] you replace yourself, outside the AI tool.
Try it now: Build at least half of your project's sections (or the core working piece) with AI drafting and you checking. Keep your build log.
You can now build a real business project with AI as your assistant and yourself as the checker.

check.q: What does a build log record?
options: What you made, which tool and what you changed
check.why: A build log shows how the project was built and checked.

check.q: You need AI to draft a customer email for your project. How do you include the customer?
options: Paste their full name and address
check.why: Placeholders keep private details out of AI.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Stage 5: Checking numbers and risks
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Check your project's numbers and make a risk checklist.
This lesson builds toward: Given your project, you will check its numbers in a spreadsheet and write a risk checklist, with every formula checked and tax and legal items marked to confirm with an official source or professional.
Every project needs honest numbers: costs (tools, time, materials), prices or savings, and when it pays off. Put them in a spreadsheet and check every formula yourself. AI can suggest what to include, but you check the math.
Then make a risk checklist from what you learned: Are all marketing and AI claims true and provable (FTC advertising rules)? Is customer data kept out of AI tools and protected? Does a person check everything customers see? Are paid promotions disclosed? Do you need a license, permit or tax registration where you operate?
For the official side, use official sites. For example, the IRS says you never have to pay a fee for an Employer Identification Number (EIN) and warns about sites that charge for one. Self-employed people generally pay self-employment tax and often quarterly estimated taxes; see irs.gov and talk to an accountant. Ask a lawyer about anything legal in your plan.
Step by step:
- List all costs, prices or savings in a spreadsheet.
- Work out when the project pays for itself.
- Check every formula yourself.
- Make a risk checklist: claims, data, human checks, disclosures, licenses and taxes.
- Mark items to confirm with an official site, accountant or lawyer.
Words to know:
- Payback: how long until money earned or saved covers what you spent.
- EIN: Employer Identification Number: a free federal tax number for a business, issued by the IRS.
- Self-employment tax: Social Security and Medicare tax that self-employed people pay.
Official sources:
- IRS: Get an Employer Identification Number
- IRS: Self-Employed Individuals Tax Center
- FTC: Advertising and Marketing Basics
Try it now: Build your numbers sheet (costs, prices or savings, payback), check every formula, and write your risk checklist with items to confirm officially.
You can now check a project's numbers and risks, and know where to confirm tax and legal points.

options: How long until earnings or savings cover the cost
check.why: Payback shows how long before the project pays for itself.

check.q: Your project needs a business license. What goes on your risk checklist?
options: Nothing; AI said it is fine
Confirm the license rules with the official agency
check.why: License and legal items are confirmed with official sources or a professional.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Stage 6: Testing, improving and presenting
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Test your finished project with real people, improve it, and present it in three minutes.
This lesson builds toward: Given your finished project, you will test it with three people, make the top changes and give a three-minute presentation, covering the problem, your solution, the proof and the next step.
Show the finished project to at least three people: the owner, a possible customer, or someone who would use it. Ask: "What is clear? What is confusing? What would you change?" For hands-on projects, have them try it.
Make the most important changes and note them. Then ask AI to help you write a three-minute presentation: the problem, who has it, your solution, the proof (what people told you and test results), the numbers, and the next step.
Practice it out loud. Ask AI to play a tough listener (an investor, a business owner, a customer) and ask you hard questions. Then put everything together as your final capstone package.
Step by step:
- Show or test the project with at least three people.
- Make the top changes and note them.
- Ask AI to outline a three-minute presentation.
- Practice out loud and time it.
- Role-play hard questions with AI.
- Assemble the final package.
Words to know:
- Pitch: a short talk that explains your project and why it matters.
- Proof: evidence that your project works, like test results and what people said.
Try it now: Final task: test your project with three people, make the top changes, practice your three-minute presentation, and assemble your capstone package: summary, full project, validation notes, numbers and risk checklist, test results and presentation.
You can now build, check, test and present a complete AI business project from start to finish.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Summary and scope The business, customer, problem or solution is missing, or the scope is too big to finish. A one-page summary with business, customer, problem and solution, and a clear scope. Explains why this project type was chosen for this business. Validation Fewer than three people, or leading questions. Notes from three or more people with exact words and each assumption marked. Shows what changed in the project because of what people said. Full project Sections are missing or unchecked AI text is left in. Every section for the project type, built with AI and checked, with a build log. The project is already in use or ready to launch. Numbers and risks Formulas unchecked or no risk checklist. Numbers sheet with checked formulas and payback, plus a risk checklist. Tax and legal items confirmed with official sources or a professional. Testing and presentation Not tested, or the presentation runs long or lacks proof. Tested with three people, top changes made, three-minute presentation with problem, solution, proof and next step. Presented out loud to a real audience and answered hard questions. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part and try again.

check.q: What is proof in a three-minute pitch?
options: Evidence such as test results and what people said
check.why: Proof shows the project works for real people.

check.q: Testers find two sections confusing. What do you do before presenting?
options: Make the top changes and test the confusing parts again
check.why: Testing is for finding and fixing problems before you present.
